intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 7 units · geology to population · drawn for a phone
This book is not “world geography” — it is **Eritrea**. Outcomes: read the land’s story (rocks), water, climate, plants and animals, soils, how people make a living, and who lives where.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Earth’s Calendar of Events

cards.title: 1.1 Introduction to the Earth’s Calendar of Events
body: At its initial stage, the earth was a globe of hot gases that finally cooled and changed into liquid.
The liquid solidified to form the solid earth.
Since then, there have been continuous uplifting, folding, volcanic eruptions and deposition.
In simple term, geology may be defined as the study of the planet earth, its rocky exterior, its history, and the processes that act upon it.

cards.title: Mnemonic — Pretty Pale Meso Ceno
body: Precambrian rocks are Eritrea’s basement (old, hard, mineral-rich). Palaeozoic left little cover here. Mesozoic = sandstones and limestones of the plateau. Cenozoic = the drama: East African Rift + opening of the Red Sea + volcanoes + Danakil sinking.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: The first rocks to be formed on the Earth due to the solidification of its crust are known as:

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the early cooling phase of Earth**
When the hot, gaseous Earth cooled, it passed into a liquid state and subsequently solidified to form the hard crust.
The first rocks crystallized directly from this process.
Since this occurred at the very beginning of geological history, these initial igneous crustal rocks are termed Precambrian or crystalline rocks.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In which geological period were the oldest sedimentary rocks containing fossilized animal remains formed?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand fossil preservation timelines**
The fossil record displays a rapid diversification of hard-bodied animals around $$500 \text{ to } 600 \text{ million years}$$ ago.

**Step 2: Identify the specific geological period**
This first major period containing abundant fossilized records of complex animal remains is defined as the Cambrian period.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct period is the **Cambrian period**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What percentage of Eritrea's surface area is covered by Precambrian crystalline basement rocks?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review the spatial distribution of basement rocks in Eritrea**
The Precambrian basement complex of Eritrea is composed of ancient metamorphic and volcanic-sedimentary successions.

**Step 2: Reference geological mappings**
Geological surveys state that these Precambrian structures are exposed or form the shallow bedrock over exactly three-fifths of the national territory.

**Step 3: Calculate the percentage**
$$\frac{3}{5} \times 100\% = 60\%$$.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The percentage coverage is **$$60\%$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which one of the following is **not true** about geological events in Eritrea?

options.A: The time from 500 to 600 million years back is known as Cambrian period.
options.B: Precambrian era is known as age of invertebrates.
options.C: In cretaceous period the Indian Ocean retreat completely from the horn of Africa.
options.D: In Cenozoic era there was immense impact on the general landforms of Eritrea.
options.E: Fossil rocks in Asmara and its surrounding are common out crops of Paleozoic era.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze Asmara's Geology.** Asmara and the surrounding central highlands of Eritrea are primarily composed of the **Precambrian Basement Complex** (metamorphic and igneous rocks like schist and granite).
**Step 2: Evaluate Statement E.** Fossil-bearing sedimentary rocks from the Paleozoic are extremely rare in Eritrea; most sedimentary rocks are Mesozoic (Adigrat Sandstone, Antalo Limestone). Asmara is definitely not a Paleozoic fossil outcrop area.
**Step 3: Conclusion.** Statement E is false.

cards.title: Geological Events in Eritrea
body: Cenozoic rifting dropped the Red Sea Trough and the Danakil Depression (an inland sea that later dried). Volcanic rocks and hot-spring / geothermal sites (e.g. Alid) are part of this young chapter.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Precambrian Era
body: As mentioned earlier, the precambrian or crystalline rocks, the oldest rocks of the earth were formed during this era when the earth was first solidified.
Mount Bizen, Gindae and north of the Nacfa area in Northern Red Sea region and Dekemhare and Segeneiti areas in Southern region.
The precambrian rocks in Eritrea can be classified into two major groups.
The metamorphic rocks include the metamorphosed precambrian rocks such as schist, gneiss, slate, greenstone, marble and phyllite.

cards.title: 1.2.2 The Palaeozoic Era
body: The weathered soils have been preserved by overlying rocks that were formed in the eras that followed.
The fossil soils hardened into rocks that lie directly over the precambrian rocks.
Outcrops of these rocks and soils include those of Asmara and its surroundings such as Tsetserat, Hazhaz, Emba Galiano, Adi Hawesha, Embeyto, Wokerti and Kutmowlie.
The upper most surface of these rocks is a red spongy material that is made up of iron oxide and kaolin. while the underlying part is clay that is partly red and partly white.

cards.title: 1.2.3 The Mesozoic Era
body: The Mesozoic Era, which is 65 to 225 million years ago, is divided into the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous Periods.
During the early stage of the Mesozoic era, i.e. the Triassic Period, the Horn of Africa began to sink gradually.
The invasion of the land by the sea continued until the Jurassic Period.
The northern limit of the advancing sea was along the Halay-DigsaGurae-Mendefera line.

cards.title: 1.2.4 Cenozoic Era
body: The Cenozoic Era extends from about 65 million years ago up to the present time.
During this era there were uplifting and faulting, eruptions, sedimentation, and the formation of the Rift Valley which had a great impact on the present landforms of Eritrea.
The Cenozoic Era includes the Tertiary and Quaternary periods.
In fact it attained its maximum limit in this period.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following represents the correct estimated age of the planet Earth?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the standard scientific estimation of Earth's age**
Based on radioactive isotope dating of meteorites and terrestrial crystalline rocks, Earth was formed approximately $$4.6 \text{ billion years}$$ ago.

**Step 2: Convert to scientific notation**
$$4.6 \text{ billion} = 4,600,000,000 = 4.6 \times 10^9$$.

**Step 3: Match with alternatives**
The correct mathematical expression is **$$4.6 \times 10^9 \text{ years}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The first rocks to be formed on the Earth due to the solidification of its crust are known as:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the early cooling phase of Earth**
When the hot, gaseous Earth cooled, it passed into a liquid state and subsequently solidified to form the hard crust. The first rocks crystallized directly from this process.

**Step 2: Relate to geological eras**
Since this occurred at the very beginning of geological history, these initial igneous crustal rocks are termed Precambrian or crystalline rocks.

**Step 3: Final Selection**
Therefore, the oldest rocks are **Precambrian crystalline rocks**.

cards.problem: Rift valleys were formed during:  A) Miocene  B) Triassic  C) Eocene  D) Paleocene  E) None

steps.text: **Step 1.** The formation of the East African Rift Valley system began during the **Miocene** epoch (approximately 22-25 million years ago) as the African plate started to split into the Nubian and Somalian plates.

glossary.meaning: A major division of geological time, made up of periods (e.g. Palaeozoic, Mesozoic, Cenozoic).
A division of a geological era, e.g. the Cambrian period of the Palaeozoic era.

tips.text: The earth, which started as a globe of hot gases, is 4.6 billion years old.
During this long period of its existence it has experienced, several changes.
The different rock formations and landforms are all the result of these changes.

The Precambrian rocks were the first to be formed when the globe of hot gases was changed into liquid and then into solid. These rocks, which are the oldest rocks, form the basis for the formation of the subsequent rocks.
In Eritrea, the Precambrian rocks cover about 60 % of the whole country.
In most cases, they are overlain by rocks of the Mesozoic and Cenozoic sediments and volcanics. However, in some areas they are also found as outcrops.
The Mesozoic deposition has led to the formation of the sandstone and limestone that cover some parts of the country.

This was followed by the fracturing of the Mesozoic surface due to the continuous uplifting which led to the out pouring of basalt and trachyte, the formation of basalt and trachyte covers, the Red Sea rift, and the drying up of the inland sea in the Danakil depression during the Cenozoic Era.
Therefore, the present rock formations and land forms of Eritrea are all the result of the geological events that occurred during the above mentioned eras, periods, and epochs.
Exam sticky notes: - Cenozoic = rift + Red Sea + Danakil

cards.front: **Tap:** Which era opened the Red Sea?
cards.back: Cenozoic. That is also why the eastern lowlands are hot, low, and still tectonically lively.
For example, the Palaeozoic Era is the age of invertebrate animals, the Mesozoic Era is the age of reptiles, and the Cenozoic Era is the age of mammals.
This period of 100 million years is called the Cambrian period.

questions.q: In which period did the Horn of Africa begin to sink and the Indian Ocean invade the land?
why: During the early stage of the Mesozoic era, i.e. the Triassic Period, the Horn of Africa began to sink gradually. As a result, the Indian Ocean invaded the land from southeast to northwest.
The invasion continued until the Jurassic, when the sea reached its northern limit (Halay–Digsa–Gurae–Mendefera line).

questions.q: Quaternary unconsolidated sediments were deposited along the Red Sea coast when:

options.B: molten materials solidified along the coast
options.C: the climate changed in the Quaternary period
options.D: the sea advanced in the Mesozoic era
options.E: Eritrea fractured in the Eocene epoch

why: In the Pleistocene epoch of the Quaternary there was an increase of rainfall – the Pluvial Period – which caused heavy erosion on the Highlands; sediments (clay, silt, sand, gravel) were deposited on the coastal areas and, with lacustrine deposits, formed the Quaternary unconsolidated sediments.
The Pluvial Period is a climatic change in the Quaternary. Heavy weathering (A) refers to the Palaeozoic; the Mesozoic sea (D) and Eocene fracturing (E) are older events.
Answer: C.

questions.q: Which one of the following is **not true** about geological events of Cenozoic era?

options.A: The uplifting of the horn of Africa gained its maximum limit during Paleocene epoch.
options.B: There was continues uplifting, sedimentation, faulting …etc. during Pliocene epoch.
options.C: Dawn warping of Hazemo plain in Oligocene epoch.
options.D: The formation of great east African rift valley during Miocene epoch.
options.E: The present era and period are Cenozoic era and quaternary period respectively.

why:
**Step 1: Analyze Epochs.** The Paleocene is the earliest epoch of the Cenozoic. Significant uplifting of the Horn of Africa and the Ethiopian/Eritrean plateaus occurred later, primarily during the Eocene, Oligocene, and reached peaks in the Miocene/Pliocene.
**Step 2: Verify other options.** B, C, D, and E are historically accurate geological descriptions of the Cenozoic era in the region.
**Step 3: Conclusion.** Statement A is false because the maximum limit was not reached as early as the Paleocene.

questions.q: Which of the following is **not** a metamorphosed Precambrian rock?
why: **Diorite** is an intrusive **igneous rock**, not a metamorphic rock. Gneiss, Schist, Phyllite, and Marble are all examples of metamorphic rocks (formed by heat and pressure).

questions.q: Which of the following statements is **not** true about the geology of Eritrea?

options.A: The Danakil Depression was once invaded by sea.
options.B: The Red Sea trough is a result of divergent movement of plates.
options.C: Most of the rocks covering the Escarpment belong to the Precambrian Era.
options.D: Rocks belonging to the Mesozoic Era cover a very large part of Eritrea.
options.E: Eritrea is considered to have some potential in geothermal energy.

why: Statement D is false because **Mesozoic rocks** (sedimentary rocks like sandstone and limestone) cover only a **small portion** of Eritrea (mainly in the Danakil and parts of the Western lowlands). The majority of Eritrea (~60%) is covered by **Precambrian** basement rocks.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which one of the following chronological order of rocks is correct from the **youngest to the oldest**?

options.A: Limestone, basalt, diorite and fossil rocks,
options.B: Trachyte, ferruginous sand stone, fossil rocks and granites
options.C: Slate, fossil rocks, upper sand stone and basalt
options.D: Fossil rocks, green stone, trachyte and limestone

why:
**Step 1: Identify Age of Rocks.** 
- **Youngest:** Cenozoic Volcanics (Trachyte, Basalt).
- **Middle:** Mesozoic Sedimentary (Sandstone, Fossiliferous Limestone).
- **Oldest:** Precambrian Basement (Granite, Diorite, Schist, Greenstone).
**Step 2: Evaluate B.** Trachyte (Cenozoic) -> Sandstone (Mesozoic) -> Fossil rocks (Mesozoic/Paleozoic) -> Granites (Precambrian). This follows the Youngest to Oldest sequence.
**Step 3: Conclusion.** B is the correct chronological order.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

why: The **Mesozoic Era** is often called the "Age of **Reptiles**" because dinosaurs and other large reptiles were the dominant life forms on Earth during this time.

options.C: Fossil rocks out crops in Asmara and its vicinity

why: In Eritrea, the **Paleozoic era** was primarily a long period of erosion and denudation, leading to the formation of peneplains. There are no significant fossil-bearing rocks from the Paleozoic era in Asmara; Asmara is situated on Precambrian basement rocks and Cenozoic volcanic basalts.
